title: A Generation That Did Not Know
subtitle: Judges 1 to 2
description: Joshua is gone, the conquest stalls tribe by tribe, and the angel at Bochim names the cycle that will run the whole book.
paragraphs: The book of Joshua closed with three burials and a generation that had seen everything. Judges opens with the words Joshua's ending held back. "After the death of Joshua, the Israelites inquired of the LORD," and their question was a soldier's question: "Who will be the first to go up and fight for us against the Canaanites?" The answer came back with a tribe's name and a promise: "Judah shall go up", answered the LORD. "Indeed, I have delivered the land into their hands."

Judah did not go alone. It invited Simeon, whose small inheritance lay inside Judah's own borders, with a trade of swords: come up with us to our territory, and we likewise will go with you to yours. The partnership worked. At Bezek they struck down ten thousand Canaanites and Perizzites, and there they caught the king whose name the place bore, Adoni-bezek, lord of Bezek. He fled, they pursued, and when they seized him they cut off his thumbs and big toes, the mutilation that ends a warrior and a king, no grip left for a sword and no footing left to stand in battle. And the prisoner read his own sentence as justice, in words the text preserves whole: "Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off have gathered the scraps under my table. As I have done to them, so God has repaid me." Seventy kings had once eaten scraps under this man's table with their hands maimed. They brought him to Jerusalem, where he died.

Judah fought Jerusalem itself and captured it, put it to the sword, and set it on fire. Then the army marched out across its whole allotment, hill country, Negev, and foothills, and at Hebron it struck down the same three names the reader met when Caleb claimed the city: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the sons of Anak. Judges retells Caleb's story here rather than assuming it, because the young man in it matters to this book. Caleb offered his daughter Achsah to whoever took Debir; his nephew Othniel took it; Achsah rode to her father and asked, "Give me a blessing". "Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well." Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs. Keep Othniel's name. He is about to become the first judge.

The victories ran on. Moses' father-in-law's descendants, the Kenites, came up with Judah from the City of Palms and settled in the Negev near Arad. Judah and Simeon together devoted Zephath to destruction and renamed it Hormah, destruction itself. Judah captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron on the coast, each with its territory.

Then the book turns, and the turn is one honest sentence long: "The LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country; but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron." The LORD was with them, and the chariots were still there. On the plains where iron decided things, the strongest tribe in Israel stopped. Joshua had told the house of Joseph, facing the same chariots, that they could drive them out. Judges records that Judah could not, and moves on without explaining how both stand. Both stand.

And Jerusalem, the city Judah had just burned? "The Benjamites, however, failed to drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem. So to this day the Jebusites live there among the Benjamites." The city lay in Benjamin's allotment, not Judah's, and a captured city is not a kept city. The Jebusites outlasted the fire and lived in Jerusalem for generations more, among the tribe that held the deed.

The house of Joseph attacked Bethel, formerly Luz, and the story there repeats the Jericho pattern with the roles thinned down to one man. Their spies caught a man leaving the city and made the old bargain: "Please show us how to get into the city, and we will treat you kindly." He showed them the entrance. The city fell to the sword, and the man and all his family were released, exactly as promised. He went to the land of the Hittites, built a city, and called it Luz, "which is its name to this day." A Canaanite city died in Canaan and was reborn under its own name somewhere else, because Israel kept its word to the one man who helped it. It is the last clean story of the chapter.

Understand what the compromise actually was, because the next chapter will name it. Forced labor is a treaty by another name: the Canaanite cities kept their walls, their fields, their altars, and their gods, and in exchange they worked. Israel got labor without obedience, income without inheritance, and neighbors whose shrines stood untouched a walk from its own doors. The command had been to tear the altars down. Labor contracts left every altar standing.

From there the chapter becomes a catalog, and the catalog is the point. Manasseh failed to drive out Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo, and their villages, "for the Canaanites were determined to dwell in that land." When Israel grew stronger it settled for forced labor, "but they never drove them out completely." Ephraim failed at Gezer, so the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer. Zebulun failed at Kitron and Nahalol; the Canaanites served as laborers and stayed. Asher failed along the whole northern coast, and the wording deepens: "So the Asherites lived among the Canaanite inhabitants of the land, because they did not drive them out." Read it twice. In Joshua the question was whether Canaanites would live among Israel. In Asher's allotment it is Israel living among Canaanites. Naphtali failed the same way. And Dan, the last name in the roll, is the only tribe the chapter shows losing ground: "The Amorites forced the Danites into the hill country and did not allow them to come down into the plain." The tribe that had marched out to take an inheritance was pushed up into the hills and penned there.

Then a messenger arrived who had not been seen since Egypt. The angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal, where the stones stood, to a place that got its name from this day, and he spoke God's charge against the whole nation: "I brought you up out of Egypt and led you into the land that I had promised to your fathers," and I said, "I will never break My covenant with you, and you are not to make a covenant with the people of this land, but you shall tear down their altars." Then the indictment, one line: "Yet you have not obeyed My voice. What is this you have done?"

The verdict reversed the conquest's direction. "So now I tell you that I will not drive out these people before you; they will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you." Joshua, dying, had warned Israel that the nations left among them would become exactly this, a snare and a trap, thorns in their eyes, if Israel clung to them. The warning had come due. "When the angel of the LORD had spoken these words to all the Israelites, the people lifted up their voices and wept." They named the place Bochim, Weeping, and offered sacrifices there. It is a real grief, and the book will test whether grief without obedience changes anything.

The narrator then reaches back and buries Joshua a second time, as if the first burial at the end of his own book were not enough to close the account. "the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel." Joshua died at 110, "the servant of the LORD," and was buried at Timnath-heres, the same inheritance town that Joshua's book spelled Timnath-serah. And then the sentence the entire book of Judges exists to explain: "After that whole generation had also been gathered to their fathers, another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel."

They did not know. The stones at Gilgal were built for exactly this, so that children would ask and fathers would answer. Within one generation the asking stopped working, and the narrator lays out the machine that would run for the rest of the book, piece by piece, like a diagram.

First the turn: "And the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals." The Baals were the storm and fertility gods of the land Israel now shared, and the Ashtoreths beside them, and the pull was agricultural and ordinary, rain and crops and the neighbors' shrines still standing because their altars had never been torn down. "Thus they forsook the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt, and they followed after various gods of the peoples around them."

Then the consequence, in the language of a market: God's anger burned, and "He delivered them into the hands of those who plundered them. He sold them into the hands of their enemies all around, whom they were no longer able to resist." The nation that had crossed the Jordan against chariots now could not stand anywhere: "Wherever Israel marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them to bring calamity, just as He had sworn to them. So they were greatly distressed."

Then the rescue, which is not earned and not explained by anything in Israel: "Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them." The judges were deliverers raised up one crisis at a time, and God was with each of them, the text says, because "the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning under those who oppressed them and afflicted them." Groaning moved Him, as it had in Egypt.

And then the relapse, the piece that makes the machine a downward spiral instead of a circle: "Israel, however, did not listen to their judges. Instead, they prostituted themselves with other gods and bowed down to them." And at each judge's death, "But when the judge died, the Israelites became even more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods to serve them and bow down to them. They would not give up their evil practices and stubborn ways." Even more corrupt than their fathers. Every turn of the cycle lands lower than the last, and the deliverers raised up inside it will show the same slide, from the clean Othniel to men Israel would barely recognize as heroes.

God's closing word in the chapter turns the leftover nations into an instrument: "Because this nation has transgressed the covenant I laid down for their fathers and has not heeded My voice, I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations Joshua left when he died. In this way I will test whether Israel will keep the way of the LORD by walking in it as their fathers did." That is why the nations remained, the narrator finishes, and why they had not been handed to Joshua all at once.

The machine is assembled. The nations left in the land have names and kings, and the first of them is already gathering an army in the east. What Israel needs is a deliverer, and the first one it gets is the young man from Debir who married Caleb's daughter, the last clean figure of Joshua's generation still standing.

title: Othniel, Ehud, and the Left Hand
subtitle: Judges 3
description: The first two deliverers: Othniel the model judge, and a left-handed Benjamite with a hidden dagger and a locked door.
paragraphs: The nations left in the land had a purpose now, and the narrator states it twice so it cannot be missed. They were left "to test all the Israelites who had not known any of the wars in Canaan," and to teach warfare to a generation that had inherited battles it never watched, "to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses." The list was the Philistines' five rulers on the coast, the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites in the Lebanon mountains. Israel's answer to the test came in three steps, each one a verse quieter than a battle: "Thus the Israelites continued to live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods." Lived among, married among, worshiped among. The cycle's first turn followed on schedule: "So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs."

Forgotten is the exact word, and the first oppressor came from the far side of the world Israel knew. God sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Aram-naharaim up in Mesopotamia, and Israel served him eight years. Eight years, then the cry the cycle runs on: "But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them."

Othniel is the model judge, and the book gives him almost no words because there is nothing wrong to record. The reader has met him twice already, taking Debir for Caleb in Joshua and again in Judges 1, marrying Achsah, settling by her springs. Now, a generation later: "The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel's judge and went out to war. And the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into the hand of Othniel, who prevailed against him." No stratagem, no speech, no flaw. "So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died." Forty years of rest is the longest a judge's generation usually gets, and it ends the way every rest in this book ends, with the deliverer's death.

"Once again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD." The second oppressor was closer and worse organized against Israel than the first. God gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, and Eglon enlisted the Ammonites and the Amalekites, Israel's oldest enemies, beat Israel in the field, and took the City of Palms, Jericho itself, the first city of the conquest, now a Moabite tax post. Israel served Eglon eighteen years, more than double the first oppression. The pattern in the numbers is the book's quiet argument: the relapses cost more each time.

"And again they cried out to the LORD, and He raised up Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, as their deliverer." Everything in that sentence is loaded. Benjamin's name means son of the right hand, and its deliverer is a man whose right hand is not his sword hand, a difference his tribe was known for; this same book will remember Benjaminite slingers as left-handed warriors, each of whom could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. Israel sent Ehud to Eglon carrying the tribute, the tax of the occupied, and Ehud prepared for the audience by making himself a weapon fitted to his difference: "Now Ehud had made for himself a double-edged sword a cubit long. He strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak." A cubit is roughly eighteen inches, a dagger more than a sword. A right-handed guard frisks the left side, where swords hang. Ehud's hung on the right, under his cloak, on the thigh nobody searched.

He presented the tribute to Eglon, "who was an obese man," and the text does not waste that detail either. The carriers were ushered out. Ehud went with them as far as the idols near Gilgal, Gilgal, of all places, where twelve stones from the Jordan still stood for the crossing, and there he turned back alone and came to the king with the oldest key in the assassin's trade, a secret: "I have a secret message for you, O king." Eglon commanded silence, and all his attendants left him.

Eglon was sitting alone in the coolness of his upper room when Ehud approached and traded the secret for a sentence: "I have a word from God for you," Ehud said, and the king rose from his seat, a mark of respect for a divine message that put his belly in reach. "And Ehud reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon's belly. Even the handle sank in after the blade, and Eglon's fat closed in over it, so that Ehud did not withdraw the sword from his belly. And Eglon's bowels emptied." The text tells it without flinching and without celebration, a king killed on his feet by the tribute-bearer he had taxed for eighteen years, dead with the weapon still in him. Ehud went out through the porch, closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him, and walked away.

What bought him his head start was the locked door and Moabite politeness. The servants found the doors locked and supplied the respectable explanation themselves: "He must be relieving himself in the cool room," they said. So they waited. The text lingers on the waiting until it curdles: "So they waited until they became worried and saw that he had still not opened the doors of the upper room. Then they took the key and opened the doors," and there was their lord lying dead on the floor.

By then Ehud had passed the idols and reached Seirah, in the hill country of Ephraim, where he blew the ram's horn, the shofar, the sound that had circled Jericho. Israel came down from the hills behind him, and his call to arms credited the victory before it happened: follow me, he told them, "for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand." They seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab and let no one cross. The Moabite force that had occupied the City of Palms was cut off from home on the far side of its own escape route, and the count is as blunt as the assassination: "At that time they struck down about ten thousand Moabites, all robust and valiant men. Not one of them escaped." Moab was subdued under Israel's hand that day, "and the land had rest for eighty years", the longest rest the book will record, won by the judge with the longest story and the strangest weapon.

Then the chapter ends with a judge who gets one verse. "After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad." An oxgoad is a farmer's stick for prodding oxen, sometimes tipped with iron. Six hundred Philistines, the coastal people with the iron, killed by a man with a farm tool, and the narrator gives him no cry, no Spirit, no rest years, just "he too saved Israel," because in this book the deliverers come in every size and the pattern does not wait for a full story.

Two turns of the cycle are complete. The oppressions ran eight years and eighteen; the rests ran forty and eighty. Read optimistically, Israel is improving. Read the way chapter 2 taught, the numbers that matter are still ahead: the next oppression will run twenty years, and it will not be a king at a distance or a fat tax collector in Jericho. It will be nine hundred iron chariots in the north, and the deliverer God raises will be a woman under a palm tree, judging Israel in the open, because the men of the story will need her courage before they find their own.

title: Deborah and the Song of Victory
subtitle: Judges 4 to 5
description: A prophetess under a palm tree, nine hundred iron chariots in the mud, and a song that tells what the battle meant.
paragraphs: "After Ehud died, the Israelites again did evil in the sight of the LORD. So the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor." Hazor. Joshua had burned that city to the ground and beheaded its king, and a generation later another Jabin reigned there over Israel, because a burned city can be rebuilt by the enemy while the victors are busy forgetting. Jabin's commander was Sisera, based at Harosheth-hagoyim, and the instrument of the oppression was the one Israel had never solved: "Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed the Israelites for twenty years." Twenty years of iron. Then the cry.

The deliverer this time was already at work before there was a war to fight. "Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. And she would sit under the Palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, where the Israelites would go up to her for judgment." Of all the judges in this book, Deborah is the only one shown doing what the title says, settling the nation's disputes in the open air, day after day, before she ever calls an army. She is prophetess and judge at once, and the war begins with her summons.

She sent for Barak son of Abinoam, from Kedesh in Naphtali, up in the north where the chariots were, and delivered God's order in God's voice: "Surely the LORD, the God of Israel, is commanding you:" "Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun. And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin's army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand."

Barak's answer has been debated ever since, and the text gives it without comment: "If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go." Read it as faith that wants God's prophet present, or as courage that needs borrowing; the text lets both stand and only records the price. "I will certainly go with you," Deborah replied, "but the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman." Selling, the cycle's own word for what God does to Israel, turned around on the oppressor. Barak went. So did Deborah. Ten thousand men of Zebulun and Naphtali gathered at Kedesh and went up Mount Tabor, a round mountain standing alone over the Jezreel plain, with Deborah among them.

The narrator plants one tent in the ground before the battle and expects the reader to remember it: "Now Heber the Kenite had moved away from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent by the great tree of Zaanannim, which was near Kedesh." A Kenite, kin to Moses by marriage, camped apart, at peace with Jabin. Remember the tent.

Sisera heard Barak was on Tabor and summoned everything: "he summoned all nine hundred of his iron chariots and all the men with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the River Kishon." Nine hundred chariots need flat, dry ground, and the Kishon valley in the dry season was a parade ground. Then Deborah gave the word that started the battle, and its confidence is total: "Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?" Barak charged downhill with ten thousand men at his back, and the prose gives the rout one agent: "And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot." The commander of nine hundred chariots left his chariot in the mud and ran. Barak pursued the army all the way back to Harosheth-hagoyim, "and the whole army of Sisera fell by the sword; not a single man was left."

All but one. Sisera ran on foot to the one address in the north where he expected safety, the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, "because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite." Jael came out to meet him with the words of hospitality: "Come in, my lord. Come in with me. Do not be afraid." She covered him with a blanket. He asked for water; "she opened a container of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him again," milk to make a tired man sleep. He set his own guard instructions before he slept: "Stand at the entrance to the tent," he said, and if anyone came asking whether a man was there, she was to say no.

The text tells what she did instead with the plainest verbs it owns. "But as he lay sleeping from exhaustion, Heber's wife Jael took a tent peg, grabbed a hammer, and went silently to Sisera. She drove the peg through his temple and into the ground, and he died." A tent peg and a workman's hammer were a tent-dwelling woman's everyday tools; pitching and striking tents was her trade. The general who had oppressed Israel for twenty years died in his sleep, in a woman's tent, killed with the tools of the house that sheltered him, outside the battle entirely, exactly where Deborah's sentence had put the honor: in the hand of a woman, and not the woman anyone expected.

Barak arrived in pursuit, and Jael went out to greet him with the day's second invitation: "Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking." He went in, "and there lay Sisera dead, with a tent peg through his temple." The chapter closes on the king, not the commander: "On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites. And the hand of the Israelites grew stronger and stronger against Jabin king of Canaan until they destroyed him."

Then Israel sang about it, and chapter 5 is the song, Deborah and Barak together, the book's own commentary on its battle. The song reaches further back than the prose does, to God marching from Seir and Sinai while "the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water." That rain is the song's explanation of the rout: the heavens opened over the Kishon, and iron chariots drown in mud. It remembers the bad years before Deborah in lines that measure what oppression did to ordinary life: "In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were deserted and the travelers took the byways. Life in the villages ceased; it ended in Israel, until I, Deborah, arose, a mother in Israel." And it names the cause the prose only implied: "When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates. Not a shield or spear was found among forty thousand in Israel."

The song does the muster roll the prose skipped, tribe by tribe, and it is not gentle with everyone. Ephraim came down, Benjamin, the commanders of Machir, the staff-bearers of Zebulun, and Issachar "rushing into the valley at his heels." But Reuben gets the same line twice, an indictment in refrain: "In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision," with its men sitting among the sheepfolds listening to the whistling for the flocks. "Gilead remained beyond the Jordan. Dan, why did you linger by the ships? Asher stayed at the coast and remained in his harbors." And one town is cursed by the angel of the LORD outright: "Curse Meroz," says the angel of the LORD. "Bitterly curse her inhabitants; for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty." Against them all the song sets the two tribes that bled: "Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield."

The battle itself the song hands to heaven: "From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera. The River Kishon swept them away, the ancient river, the River Kishon." Then it turns to Jael and gives her the song's highest title: "Most blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, most blessed of tent-dwelling women." "He asked for water, and she gave him milk." And it sings the killing three times over in falling lines, ending flat: "where he collapsed, there he fell dead."

The song's last scene is its coldest. It sets a window in Harosheth or Hazor and a mother looking through the lattice, asking the question the whole song has already answered: "Why is his chariot so long in coming? What has delayed the clatter of his chariots?" Her ladies comfort her with the arithmetic of plunder, imagining the army dividing spoil, "a girl or two for each warrior," dyed and embroidered cloth for Sisera's neck. The reader knows what the window does not: the chariot is empty in the mud, the general is dead in a tent, and the woman who killed him has been pronounced most blessed among women by the nation he oppressed. The song does not pity the mother or mock her. It lets her keep looking out the window, and ends: "So may all Your enemies perish, O LORD! But may those who love You shine like the sun at its brightest." And the land had rest for forty years.

Prose told what happened; the song told what it meant, and the two accounts keep their own details, Meroz and the muster roll on one side, the blanket and the milk on the other. Neither is corrected by the other. That is how this book remembers: a battle and a song about the battle, standing side by side, both true in the way they were given. The rest will last forty years. When it ends, the oppressor will not be a king with chariots but a swarm out of the desert that eats Israel's harvest year after year, and the deliverer will be found hiding from it, threshing wheat in a winepress.

title: Gideon: Fleece, and Three Hundred
subtitle: Judges 6 to 7
description: A frightened man threshing wheat in a winepress is called a mighty man of valor, and his army is sent home until three hundred remain.
paragraphs: The next oppression was not an army that came and fought. It was a system that came and ate. "Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; so He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years." Midianites, Amalekites, and the people of the east timed their invasions to the harvest: "Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other people of the east would come up and invade them, encamping against them as far as Gaza and destroying the produce of the land. They left Israel with no sustenance, neither sheep nor oxen nor donkeys." They came "like a great swarm of locusts," with innumerable camels, and Israel lived in the holes of its own country, "shelters for themselves in the mountains, caves, and strongholds." Seven years of planting for someone else. "Israel was greatly impoverished by Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD."

This time God answered the cry first with a prophet, not a deliverer, and the prophet brought a diagnosis instead of an army: "I brought you up out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. I delivered you out of the hands of Egypt and all your oppressors. I drove them out before you and gave you their land." Then the charge, with the people's own gardens in view: "I am the LORD your God. You must not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell." And the verdict: "But you did not obey Me." No new information. Israel knew the story by heart. That was the problem the whole book keeps circling: knowing was not the same as obeying, and a generation that had been told everything was starving anyway.

The deliverer, when he came, was found hiding from the oppression he was meant to end. The angel of the LORD sat under the oak at Ophrah, "where his son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites." A winepress is a pit. You thresh wheat on an open floor where the wind takes the chaff; Gideon was doing it underground, in secret, a cupful at a time. Into that pit the angel spoke the most unlikely sentence in the book so far: "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."

Gideon's reply is the honest argument of a man who knows the family stories and cannot square them with the winepress: "Please, my Lord," Gideon replied, "if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? And where are all His wonders of which our fathers told us, saying," and here Gideon quotes the fathers the way the fathers were quoted at every table in Israel: "Has not the LORD brought us up out of Egypt?" Then his own conclusion, flat as a stone: "But now the LORD has forsaken us and delivered us into the hand of Midian."

God did not answer the argument. He answered the man. "Go in the strength you have and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Am I not sending you?" Gideon laid out his credentials, which were a list of smallness: "how can I save Israel? Indeed, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father's house." And the promise that carries the whole Gideon story was given, the same one given to Moses at a bush and to Joshua at a river: "Surely I will be with you," the LORD replied, "and you will strike down all the Midianites as one man."

Gideon asked for a sign and brought an offering, a young goat, unleavened bread, a pot of broth, and the angel had him lay it on a rock and pour the broth over it. The staff touched the food, "and fire flared from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened bread. Then the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight." Gideon knew then what he had been talking to, and terror replaced argument: "Oh no, Lord GOD! I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face!" The answer was the name of the altar Gideon built on the spot: "Peace be with you. Do not be afraid, for you will not die." He called the altar The LORD Is Peace, and the text says it stood in Ophrah to the narrator's own day.

That night the commission stopped being theoretical. Gideon was ordered to tear down his own father's altar to Baal and cut down the Asherah pole beside it, and to build a proper altar to the LORD on the stronghold and offer his father's second bull on it, with the Asherah's wood for fuel. He did it, with ten servants, and the text states his fear as plainly as his obedience: "But because he was too afraid of his father's household and the men of the city, he did it by night rather than in the daytime." The first battle of the deliverer was against his father's gods, fought at midnight, and it counts in the text as done.

Morning brought the city to Joash's door demanding his son's death for the ruined altar. Joash, whose altar it had been, defended the son who destroyed it with the sharpest logic in the chapter: "Are you contending for Baal? Are you trying to save him? Whoever pleads his case will be put to death by morning! If Baal is a god, let him contend for himself with the one who has torn down his altar." If Baal needs a mob, he is no god; if he is a god, he needs no mob. Gideon walked out of that morning with a new name, Jerubbaal, let Baal contend with him, and the name stuck to him for the rest of the book, the recorder using both names as if the dare were his title.

Then the invasion came in force, Midian and Amalek and the east crossing the Jordan and camping in the Valley of Jezreel, and the pattern of the cycle finally turned: "So the Spirit of the LORD came upon Gideon, who blew the ram's horn and rallied the Abiezrites behind him." Messengers went through Manasseh and to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and this time the tribes came up. And Gideon, with an army finally gathering behind him, asked God for the sign everyone remembers, and he asked it in full knowledge of how it sounded: "If You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said, then behold, I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that You are going to save Israel by my hand, as You have said." Morning: wet fleece, dry ground, a bowlful of water wrung out. Then the request reversed, with its own apology built in: "Do not be angry with me; let me speak one more time. Please allow me one more test with the fleece. This time let it be dry, and the ground covered with dew." And that night God did so. The book does not rebuke the fleece. It records a frightened man asking twice and a God answering twice, and then it takes the frightened man's army away from him in stages, which is a harder test than the fleece ever was.

At the spring of Harod, with Midian camped north in the valley by the hill of Moreh, God announced the reduction and its reason: "You have too many men for Me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying," and the sentence God would not let Israel say is the sentence every other victory in the ancient world ended with: "My own hand has saved me." So the fearful were invited to leave, using the law Moses had given for exactly this, and twenty-two thousand men turned back. Ten thousand remained. "There are still too many men." Down at the water God sifted them by how they drank: those who lapped water with their tongues like dogs, scooping with their hands to their mouths, against those who knelt down to drink. The lappers numbered three hundred. "With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver the Midianites into your hand. But all the others are to go home." Thirty-two thousand had become three hundred, and the three hundred took the provisions and the rams' horns of the men sent home, horns and food for an army that was about to fight with noise and light instead of numbers.

That night God offered the frightened commander one more kindness, unasked: "Get up and go down against the camp, for I have delivered it into your hand. But if you are afraid to do so, then go down to the camp with your servant Purah and listen to what they are saying." Gideon went down, because he was afraid, and at the outposts of a camp lying in the valley "like a swarm of locusts," with camels "as countless as the sand on the seashore," he heard an enemy soldier tell a dream: "Behold, I had a dream," he said, "and I saw a loaf of barley bread come tumbling into the Midianite camp. It struck the tent so hard that the tent overturned and collapsed." Barley bread, the poor man's loaf, a nobody's food, rolling into the camp of kings. And the friend interpreted it on the spot, by name: "This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand." Gideon, who had asked God for sign after sign, received the last one from the enemy's own mouth, and he bowed in worship in the dark outside the camp of the men who feared him.

The battle, when it came, was mostly sound and light. Three hundred men in three companies, each with a ram's horn in one hand and a large jar holding a torch in the other, took positions around the camp. "Watch me and do as I do," Gideon said. "When I and all who are with me blow our horns, then you are also to blow your horns from all around the camp and shout," and the shout he gave them put God's name first: "For the LORD and for Gideon!" At the beginning of the middle watch, just after the guard changed, three hundred horns blew at once and three hundred jars smashed, torches flaring out of the dark on every side, and the cry went up: "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!" The text is careful about what the three hundred did next: "Each Israelite took his position around the camp, and the entire Midianite army fled, crying out as they ran." They stood still. The camp did the rest: "And when the three hundred rams' horns sounded, the LORD set all the men in the camp against one another with their swords." An army of locusts woke in darkness to horns and fire on every side, assumed a vast force had surrounded it, and killed itself.

The fugitives ran for the Jordan, and now the tribes Gideon had sent home entered the story he had been reduced to win without them: men of Naphtali, Asher, and Manasseh were called out in pursuit, and Ephraim seized the waters of the Jordan ahead of the fugitives as far as Beth-barah. Ephraim also captured Midian's two princes, Oreb and Zeeb, raven and wolf, and killed them, Oreb at the rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb, places that took their names from the deaths. They brought the heads of the two princes to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan. The winepress Gideon hid in has become a place where a Midianite prince died, and the deliverer is across the river now, in pursuit, holding the heads of princes, and about to discover that victory has its own dangers: the men of Ephraim are coming to him angry, and what he does with the next few conversations will shape the rest of his life.

title: Gideon's Ephod, and Abimelech
subtitle: Judges 8 to 9
description: Gideon refuses a crown and builds a snare of gold, and his son buys a kingship with temple silver and one stone.
paragraphs: Victory produced its first conflict before the pursuit even ended, and it came from inside Israel. The men of Ephraim met Gideon with a grievance sharpened into a fight: "Why have you done this to us? Why did you fail to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they contended with him violently. Ephraim was the proud central tribe, called late, handed the Jordan crossings and the two princes, and still insulted at missing the opening battle. Gideon's answer is a small masterpiece of defusing, and every word of it is honor handed over in public: "Now what have I accomplished compared to you? Are not the gleanings of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? God has delivered Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, into your hand. What was I able to do compared to you?" Your leftovers outweigh my whole harvest; God gave you the princes; what was I beside you? "When he had said this, their anger against him subsided." Diplomacy worked. Remember that it worked, because east of the Jordan Gideon stops using it.

He crossed the river with his three hundred, "exhausted yet still in pursuit," chasing the two kings of Midian who were still at large, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he asked the Israelite town of Succoth for bread for his men. Succoth's leaders refused with a taunt disguised as a question: "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?" Show us the kings in chains, then we'll feed you. They were hedging, keeping Midian's favor available if Gideon lost, and Gideon heard the hedge and answered it with a threat he fully intended to keep, and the threat was a promise: "when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will tear your flesh with the thorns and briers of the wilderness!" Penuel, the next town up, gave the same answer and got its own sentence: "When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!"

The kings were at Karkor with fifteen thousand men, all that remained of a host of a hundred and thirty-five thousand swordsmen. Gideon came up by the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah and hit the camp by surprise, and captured Zebah and Zalmunna alive, exactly the proof Succoth had demanded. On the way back he caught a young man of Succoth and interrogated him, and the young man wrote down the names of the town's seventy-seven leaders and elders, a list made to be used. Gideon presented the kings to the men who had refused him bread and quoted their own taunt back at them with the evidence standing beside him, and then he kept his word: "Then he took the elders of the city, and using the thorns and briers of the wilderness, he disciplined the men of Succoth." At Penuel he pulled down the tower and killed the men of the city. Read the two halves of the chapter against each other and the slide is right there in the hero. West of the Jordan, insulted by Ephraim's pride, Gideon answered with humility and made peace. East of it, refused by frightened Israelite towns, he answered with thorns and a demolished tower and dead Israelites. The deliverer is starting to punish the delivered.

One account remained, and it was personal. Gideon asked the captured kings what kind of men they had killed at Tabor, and their answer sealed them: "Men like you," they answered, "each one resembling the son of a king." "They were my brothers," Gideon replied, "the sons of my mother! As surely as the LORD lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you." He ordered his firstborn Jether to execute them, and the boy would not draw his sword, "he was fearful because he was still a youth," a frightened son of a father who once hid in a winepress and tore down an altar at night for fear. The kings asked for the cleaner death themselves: "Get up and kill us yourself, for as the man is, so is his strength." Gideon killed them, and took the crescent ornaments from their camels' necks. It is the first gold he takes in the chapter. It is not the last.

Then Israel made the offer the whole era had been circling: "Rule over us, you and your son and grandson, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." A hereditary kingship, offered by acclamation to the deliverer. Gideon's refusal is the theological high ground of the book: "I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you." And in the very next breath he made his request: an earring from every man's plunder. They gave gladly, a garment spread out and gold thrown onto it, until the earrings alone weighed 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescents and pendants and purple garments of the kings. "From all this Gideon made an ephod, which he placed in Ophrah, his hometown. But soon all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and his household."

Hold the two acts side by side, because the text does. The man who would not be king built a golden shrine in his hometown and all Israel came to worship at it. He refused the title and took the trappings: seventy sons by many wives, a royal household in everything but name, and a concubine in Shechem who bore him a son he named Abimelech, which means my father is king. The refusal was real words. The life was a court's life. And the land rested forty years in the days of Gideon, and he died at a ripe old age and was buried in his father's tomb at Ophrah, and the machine turned instantly: "And as soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned and prostituted themselves with the Baals, and they set up Baal-berith as their god. The Israelites failed to remember the LORD their God who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies on every side. They did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) for all the good things he had done for Israel."

The ingratitude had a beneficiary, and he moved fast. Abimelech went to Shechem, to his mother's clan, with a pitch built on blood and arithmetic. Ask all the leaders of Shechem, he told them: "Is it better for you that seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or just one man?" And remind them: "Remember that I am your own flesh and blood." The leaders' hearts inclined to him for the reason he had scripted: "He is our brother." They funded the coup out of the temple treasury of Baal-berith, seventy shekels of silver, with which Abimelech "hired some worthless and reckless men to follow him." Then he went home to Ophrah and did the thing the pitch had promised to prevent anyone else from doing: "He went to his father's house in Ophrah, and on one stone murdered his seventy brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, survived, because he hid himself." Seventy shekels, seventy brothers, one stone. The leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo crowned the survivor's murderer king beside the oak at the pillar in Shechem, in the city where Jacob had buried idols under an oak and Joshua had renewed the covenant under one.

Jotham, the one who hid, climbed Mount Gerizim, the mountain of blessing from the covenant ceremony, and shouted a parable down at the coronation. The trees went out to anoint a king. The olive tree refused: "Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?" The fig tree refused its sweetness, the vine refused its wine, each too fruitful to rule. Finally all the trees said to the thornbush the words the fruitful trees had refused under: "Come and reign over us." And the thornbush, the one plant with nothing to give but shade it does not have and fire it does, accepted with a threat: "If you really are anointing me as king over you, come and find refuge in my shade. But if not, may fire come out of the thornbush and consume the cedars of Lebanon." Jotham then applied it without flinching, rehearsing Gideon's rescue and the stone, and laid the terms: if Shechem had acted honestly, rejoice in Abimelech. "But if not, may fire come from Abimelech and consume the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo, and may fire come from the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo and consume Abimelech." He ran for his life to Beer, and the curse hung over the city for three years, waiting for its fuel.

It came on schedule, and the text assigns the arsonist openly: after three years "God sent a spirit of animosity between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem," so that the crime against the seventy sons might come to justice and their blood be avenged on both the murderer and the men who had funded him. Shechem's leaders began ambushing travelers on the hilltops to rob Abimelech's revenue, and into the rot walked Gaal son of Ebed, a loud newcomer who won the city at a harvest festival in the house of their god, drinking and cursing Abimelech between courses: "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? You are to serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem. Why should we serve Abimelech?" Zebul, Abimelech's governor, heard it and sent a warning by night, and Abimelech came with four companies and lay in the fields till sunrise.

The morning scene is almost comedy played over a grave. Gaal stood at the gate and saw men coming down the hills and reported it, and Zebul stalled him with a sneer: "The shadows of the mountains look like men to you." When Gaal insisted, people coming down by the Diviners' Oak, Zebul dropped the act: "Where is your gloating now?" Then he threw Gaal's own festival words back at him: "Who is Abimelech that we should serve him?" "Are these not the people you ridiculed? Go out now and fight them!" Gaal fought, broke, and fled, and Zebul drove him and his brothers out of Shechem. The next day Abimelech ambushed the city folk in their fields, took the city, killed its people, demolished it, and sowed it with salt, a curse plowed into the ground so nothing would grow there again. Jotham's fire had begun moving, and it moved in both directions exactly as pronounced.

The leaders who had crowned him fled into the inner chamber of the temple of El-berith in the tower of Shechem, about a thousand men and women, and Abimelech repeated their own coronation gift back to them as fuel. On Mount Zalmon he cut a branch with his axe, hoisted it on his shoulder, and told his men: "Hurry and do what you have seen me do." They piled the branches against the chamber and burned it over the people inside. Every leader who had said "He is our brother" died by fire from Abimelech's hand. Then he marched on Thebez and took it, and its people fled to a strong tower inside the city, and Abimelech came up to its entrance to set the same fire a second time.

This time the tower answered. "But a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech's head, crushing his skull." A millstone, a kitchen stone, dropped by an unnamed woman from a roof, the second woman in the book to kill a commander from above while he attacked. Dying, Abimelech's last thought was for the wording of his death: "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me," and his fear names itself in his own quoted words, a woman killed him. His armor-bearer ran him through, and he died by an Israelite sword with a woman's millstone as the cause, both halves of his shame preserved. "And when the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went home." No rest is recorded. No judge is named. The narrator closes the account with the audit instead: "In this way God repaid the wickedness that Abimelech had done to his father in murdering his seventy brothers. And God also brought all the wickedness of the men of Shechem back upon their own heads. So the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them."

Israel's first king was never raised up by God, never anointed, never called a judge. He was a deliverer's son who bought a crown with temple silver and held it three years by murder, and the fire his half brother promised from Gerizim consumed the buyers and the bought alike. The book pauses now for two quiet judges whose whole records fit in a few verses, Tola and Jair, and then the cycle turns again, and this time when Israel cries, God answers the cry with an argument before He answers it with a deliverer.

title: Jephthah and the Vow
subtitle: Judges 10 to 12
description: The outcast son argues like a statesman, wins his war, and meets the price of a careless vow at his own door.
paragraphs: After Abimelech the book breathes twice, quietly. Tola of Issachar rose up to save Israel and judged twenty-three years from Shamir in Ephraim's hills, and no war of his is recorded at all. Jair the Gileadite followed for twenty-two years, and his record is a family's prosperity: thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys and held thirty towns in Gilead called Havvoth-jair, the towns of Jair, to this day. Forty-five years of judges with no oppressor named. Then Jair died, and the cycle turned to its lowest point yet.

"And again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals, the Ashtoreths, the gods of Aram, Sidon, and Moab, and the gods of the Ammonites and Philistines. Thus they forsook the LORD and did not serve Him." Count the gods. Earlier turns named Baals and Ashtoreths; this one catalogs the whole neighborhood's pantheon, seven directions of idolatry at once, as if Israel were collecting. The consequence matched: God sold them into two hands at once, the Philistines on the coast and the Ammonites in the east, and the Ammonites "harassed and oppressed the Israelites" in Gilead for eighteen years, then crossed the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim too, "and Israel was in deep distress."

Israel cried out with the standard confession, "We have sinned against You, for we have indeed forsaken our God and served the Baals," and this time God argued with the cry. His answer is a courtroom recital of the whole book so far, oppressor by oppressor: "When the Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, and Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to Me, did I not save you from their hands? But you have forsaken Me and served other gods, so I will no longer save you." Then the sentence no other generation in the book had heard: "Go and cry out to the gods you have chosen. Let them save you in your time of trouble."

What Israel did next is the one genuinely new thing in the cycle. The confession deepened past formula: "We have sinned," the Israelites said to the LORD. "Deal with us as You see fit; but please deliver us today!" Accept any punishment, only save us. And then they acted on it before any deliverer appeared: "So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and He could no longer bear the misery of Israel." Every previous turn had God moved to pity by groaning. This one says He could no longer bear it, after they had first borne the cost of putting the gods away. The Ammonites mustered in Gilead; Israel camped at Mizpah; and Gilead's rulers posted the command like a notice: "Whoever will launch the attack against the Ammonites will be the head of all who live in Gilead."

The man they found for the job was the one they had thrown away. "Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valor; he was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was his father." His father's legitimate sons had grown up and driven him out with a sentence that cut him off from the family estate: "You shall have no inheritance in our father's house, because you are the son of another woman." Jephthah fled to the land of Tob, and there "worthless men gathered around him and traveled with him," the same word the book used for Abimelech's hired swords, except Abimelech bought his worthless men with temple silver and Jephthah's gathered to him for nothing, because an outcast with a sword draws outcasts.

When Ammon made war, the elders of Gilead went to Tob to fetch him, and their offer was blunt: come, they said, "be our commander, so that we can fight against the Ammonites." Jephthah made them own their history before he took the job: "Did you not hate me and expel me from my father's house? Why then have you come to me now, when you are in distress?" They raised the offer to the exact terms of the Mizpah notice, commander and head over all Gilead, and Jephthah locked it with an oath: "If you take me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them to me, will I really be your leader?" "The LORD is our witness if we do not do as you say." Then he went with them, and at Mizpah he "repeated all his terms in the presence of the LORD," a contract sworn at the same camp where God's refusal speech was still ringing. Gilead's rejected son came home as its head, with God as the witness of the bargain.

Jephthah's first weapon was not a sword. It was a history brief, sent by messengers to the king of Ammon, answering Ammon's land claim with three hundred years of receipts. Israel had not taken Moab's or Ammon's land; it had asked Edom and Moab for passage and been refused; it had taken the Amorite king Sihon's land only after Sihon attacked, land God had given: "Now since the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites from before His people Israel, should you now possess it?" He pressed the theology of the region back at the king without flinching: "Do you not possess whatever your god Chemosh grants you? So also, we possess whatever the LORD our God has granted us." He cited Balak, who had never fought Israel over this land. He cited the calendar: "For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon, Aroer, and their villages, as well as all the cities along the banks of the Arnon. Why did you not take them back during that time?" And he closed by handing the case upward: "I have not sinned against you, but you have done me wrong by waging war against me. May the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites." The king of the Ammonites paid no heed. But the record stands: the outcast from Tob argued Israel's title like a statesman before he fought like a soldier, and when the fighting came, the text gives the sequence its full weight: "Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, then through Mizpah of Gilead. And from there he advanced against the Ammonites."

Then, in the advance, Jephthah made the vow. It is quoted here exactly, because everything after it turns on its wording: "If indeed You will deliver the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out the door of my house to greet me on my triumphant return from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering." Whatever comes out the door. In a house with servants, animals, and one child, the vow left the greeter to chance, or to God, which is the same gamble Gideon never took: Gideon asked God for signs; Jephthah offered God a blank check drawn on whoever loved him enough to run out first.

God delivered the Ammonites into his hand. The campaign was a rout, twenty cities devastated "from Aroer to the vicinity of Minnith, as far as Abel-keramim," and the Ammonites were subdued before Israel. Jephthah came home to Mizpah a victor and a head of Gilead, and the door of his house opened: "And when Jephthah returned home to Mizpah, there was his daughter coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing! She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her." The exclamation point is the narrator's own. Tambourines and dancing were how Israel's women had always greeted victory, Miriam at the sea, the women for Saul and David in a later day. Jephthah's only child came out doing the most natural thing in the world, and her father tore his clothes: "No! Not my daughter! You have brought me to my knees! You have brought great misery upon me, for I have given my word to the LORD and cannot take it back."

Her answer is the most composed speech in the chapter, and it comes from the person with the least power in it: She replied to her father: "you have given your word to the LORD. Do to me as you have said, for the LORD has avenged you of your enemies, the Ammonites." She asked one thing, and the thing she asked names what the vow was costing her: "Let me do this one thing: Let me wander for two months through the mountains with my friends and mourn my virginity." Not her life in the abstract, her unlived life, the marriage and children that would now never happen, the end of her father's line in her, the outcast's house closing with her. He told her to go, and she went to the mountains with her friends for two months.

"After two months, she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. And she had never had relations with a man." That is all the text says, and its restraint deserves to be met with restraint. The narrative does not describe the act, does not praise it, and does not condemn it in so many words; it records that Jephthah did as he had vowed, and then it records what Israel did with the memory: "it has become a custom in Israel that each year the young women of Israel go out for four days to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite." Lament, not celebrate. The daughters of Israel kept four days a year for her, for generations, and the book moves on leaving the verdict to that lament and to the vow's own arithmetic: a leader who had bargained brilliantly with elders and kings bargained carelessly once with God, and the price came out his door dancing. Readers have argued for three thousand years about what exactly happened on that return, and the honest place to leave it is where the text leaves it: he did to her as he had vowed, and she had never known a man, and Israel's daughters wept for her every year.

Ephraim arrived after the victory, as Ephraim now reliably did, and this time there was no gleaning speech. They crossed to Zaphon with a threat uglier than Gideon's day: "Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down with you inside!" Jephthah, who knew something about being burned out of a father's house, answered with facts instead of flattery: "My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands. When I saw that you would not save me, I risked my life and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why then have you come today to fight against me?" Ephraim fought anyway, and added an insult to the charge, calling the Gileadites fugitives living in Ephraim and Manasseh's territory, and Gilead struck them down and took the fords of the Jordan, Ehud's old tactic turned inward on Israel itself.

At the fords they ran a test of accent. Whenever a fugitive Ephraimite asked to cross, the Gileadites asked if he was an Ephraimite, and if he said no, they told him to say Shibboleth. If he said Sibboleth, because he could not pronounce it correctly, they seized him and killed him at the fords. One consonant was the difference between the two sides of the river, and "at that time 42,000 Ephraimites were killed." Forty-two thousand Israelites dead in a civil quarrel, at the same river crossings where God had once opened the water for the whole nation together. Jephthah judged Israel six years, the shortest tenure of any major judge so far, and died and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.

Three quiet men close the section. Ibzan of Bethlehem judged seven years, and his record is a web of marriages, thirty sons and thirty daughters, the daughters married out of the clan and thirty wives brought in for the sons, alliance by wedding on a scale no warrior in the book matches. Elon the Zebulunite judged ten years and has nothing recorded but his burial. Abdon son of Hillel judged eight years, with forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys, Jair's prosperity pattern repeated. Then the cycle is due to turn again, and the deliverer for the next turn will be the most gifted and least governed man in the book, announced by an angel before his birth, set apart from the womb, and strong enough to tear a lion apart with his hands. The tragedy the book is building toward is not that Israel lacks a strong deliverer. It is that strength is all the next one has.

title: Samson: The Riddle and the Foxes
subtitle: Judges 13 to 15
description: Announced before his birth and set apart from the womb, Samson begins a deliverance fought mostly as a private feud.
paragraphs: The longest oppression in the book gets the quietest opening. "Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD, so He delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years." Forty years, and for the first time in the cycle the text records no cry. Israel had stopped groaning. The Philistines were not a raid or a tax anymore; they were the weather. And into that silence, before any deliverer was asked for, God sent an announcement to a barren woman in Zorah, of the clan of Dan, the tribe the Amorites had penned into the hills in Judges 1.

The angel of the LORD appeared to the wife of Manoah with a promise and a regimen in the same breath: "It is true that you are barren and have no children; but you will conceive and give birth to a son. Now please be careful not to drink wine or strong drink, and not to eat anything unclean. For behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son. And no razor shall touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines." Begin. Hold that word against everything Samson does. No deliverer before him was given a partial assignment; Othniel finished his war, Ehud finished his. Samson's commission is to begin a deliverance that Israel would need another generation and a king to complete, and the Nazirite vow over him, no razor, no wine, no unclean food, begins before he is born and binds his mother first.

She reported it to her husband with a field report's plainness: "A man of God came to me. His appearance was like the angel of God, exceedingly awesome." Manoah prayed for a second visit, and his prayer is the most parental sentence in the book: "Please, O Lord, let the man of God You sent us come to us again to teach us how to raise the boy who is to be born." The angel returned, to the woman again, in the field, and Manoah ran after her and asked the practical question: "When your words come to pass, what will be the boy's rule of life and mission?" The answer repeated the regimen and added nothing. When Manoah pressed for hospitality and then for the visitor's name, he got the refusal that tells him who he is hosting: "Why do you ask my name," said the angel of the LORD, "since it is beyond comprehension?" The goat and grain offering went onto a rock, the flame rose, and "the angel of the LORD ascended in the flame." Manoah fell apart in the correct theological direction: "We are going to die," he said to his wife, "for we have seen God!" And his wife out-reasoned him, the second woman in this book to be its calmest theologian: "If the LORD had intended to kill us, He would not have accepted the burnt offering and the grain offering from our hands, nor would He have shown us all these things or spoken to us this way." The boy was born and named Samson, and the LORD blessed him, and the Spirit of the LORD "began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol." Stir is the text's word, an unsettled pushing, and it is the right word for everything that follows.

Samson's first recorded act as a grown man is a demand. Down in Timnah, a Philistine town a few miles from home, he saw a woman, and came home and told his parents: "I have seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah. Now get her for me as a wife." His parents objected on the exact ground the book has been building since Joshua: "Can't you find a young woman among your relatives or among any of our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?" Samson's answer is the creed of the whole era in one line, though he applies it only to himself: "Get her for me, for she is pleasing to my eyes." Right in his own eyes. The narrator steps in with the book's most startling parenthesis: his parents did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion against the Philistines. God intended to use the marriage as a provocation. It changes nothing about the marriage's wisdom; it explains its place in the war.

On the road down to Timnah, at the vineyards, a young lion came roaring at him, "and the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him, and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands as one would tear a young goat." A Nazirite at a vineyard, where his vow said he should not be, kills a lion with strength that arrives like weather. He told no one. Later, returning to take the woman, he turned aside to see the carcass and found bees and honey in it, death housing sweetness, and he ate, and fed his parents, "but he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion's carcass." A Nazirite must not touch a dead body, any dead body; Samson scooped honey out of one and served it at home. The vow is eroding in private, in small spoonfuls, long before Delilah.

The wedding feast ran seven days, with thirty Philistine companions assigned to the bridegroom, and Samson entertained them with a wager: "Let me tell you a riddle," Samson said to them. "If you can solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes. But if you cannot solve it, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes." "Tell us your riddle," they replied. "Let us hear it." The riddle was his secret, unwitnessed and therefore unfair, a lion and honey nobody else had seen: "Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet." Three days they worked at it and failed. On the fourth day the companions went around Samson to his wife with the book's recurring currency, fire: "Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father's household to death. Did you invite us here to rob us?"

She wept on him for the rest of the feast, with the argument every spouse in the book seems to use sooner or later: "You hate me! You do not really love me! You have posed to my people a riddle, but have not explained it to me." Samson's first defense was sound: "I have not even explained it to my father or mother, so why should I explain it to you?" But seven days of tears outlasted it. On the seventh day, "because she had pressed him so much, he told her the answer. And in turn she explained the riddle to her people." Before sunset the men of the city presented their solution as a counter-riddle: "What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?" Samson's answer named what they had done in the language of the farm: "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have solved my riddle!"

Then the Spirit came mightily on him, and the deliverance God had promised to begin looked like this: he went down to Ashkelon, a Philistine city miles away, killed thirty of its men, stripped their clothes, and paid his wager with them. Thirty men who had never heard the riddle died for it. "And burning with anger, Samson returned to his father's house," and his wife was given to one of the companions, the best man. The occasion God sought had arrived, and it looked less like a war of liberation than a feud, which is precisely the texture of Samson's whole judgeship: the Spirit's power and the man's appetites pulling the same chariot.

Some time later, at wheat harvest, Samson took a young goat as a peace offering and went to visit his wife, expecting to go in to her. Her father blocked the door: "I was sure that you thoroughly hated her," said her father, "so I gave her to one of the men who accompanied you. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead." Samson's reply draws the line he would operate on for the rest of his life: "This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines." This time. The retaliation ladder starts here, and every rung of it will be, in Samson's accounting, the Philistines' fault. He caught three hundred foxes, tied them tail to tail in pairs with a torch fastened between each pair, lit the torches, and let them run through the standing grain of the Philistines at harvest, "burning up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves." Food, wine, and oil in one fire. When the Philistines learned why, that the Timnite's daughter had been given to another man, they went up and burned her and her father to death, carrying out on Samson's wife the exact threat her cooperation was meant to escape. The book does not pause over her. It lets the arithmetic speak: she betrayed her husband to avoid being burned, and was burned anyway, by her own people, for being betrayed by her father.

Samson's vengeance for that was personal and announced: "Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you." He struck them "ruthlessly with a great slaughter," and withdrew to a cave in the rock of Etam, inside Judah's own territory. The Philistines camped in Judah and deployed near Lehi, and when Judah asked why, the answer was an arrest warrant: they had come to seize Samson and repay him. Here the book delivers its verdict on the forty years, not through a prophet but through Israel's own troops. Three thousand men of Judah went down to Etam, not to join Samson but to arrest him: "Do you not realize that the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?" Three thousand Israelites against one Israelite, on behalf of the Philistines. Samson's reply is the feud's whole logic in one sentence: "I have done to them what they did to me," he replied. He made them swear not to kill him themselves, and let his own tribe bind him with two new ropes and carry him up to the enemy like tribute.

At Lehi the Philistines came out shouting, "and the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him. The ropes on his arms became like burnt flax, and the bonds broke loose from his hands." He found the fresh jawbone of a donkey, another dead thing in the Nazirite's hand, "and struck down a thousand men." Then he sang, the only song of his the book records, two lines of wordplay on the word for donkey and the word for heap: "With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps. With the jawbone of a donkey I have slain a thousand men." He named the place Ramath-lehi, jawbone hill, threw the bone away, and immediately nearly died of the most ordinary need in the world. His prayer, when it finally comes, is the first time Samson speaks to God in the book, and it is a complaint with a claim staked on it: "You have accomplished this great deliverance through Your servant. Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?" God split open a hollow place in Lehi and water came out, and Samson drank and revived, and named it En-hakkore, the spring of the one who called. It stands in Lehi to this day, says the narrator.

"And Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines." Twenty of the forty years of oppression, with the deliverance still only begun, its champion a man who had never led an army, never summoned a tribe, never held a court under a palm tree, fighting a private war at irregular intervals with whatever came to hand. Israel had not cried out, and God had sent a deliverer anyway, and the deliverer was a riddle in the shape of a man: a Nazirite who ate from a corpse, a judge who took no counsel, strength without a governor on it. The Philistines had learned to fear his arms. What none of them yet knew, Israelite or Philistine, was that the way through Samson was never his strength. It was his tongue, loosened by whoever shared his pillow, and the next woman in his life would not stop at one secret.

title: Samson and Delilah
subtitle: Judges 16
description: The secret is pressed out of him on Delilah's lap, and the blind prisoner prays once more between the pillars.
paragraphs: One day Samson went down to Gaza, the southernmost of the Philistines' five cities, and saw a prostitute and went in to her. Word reached the Gazites, and they surrounded the place and lay in wait at the city gate all night, keeping quiet, planning to kill him at dawn. Samson did not stay the night. "But Samson lay there only until midnight, when he got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and both gateposts, and pulled them out, bar and all. Then he put them on his shoulders and took them to the top of the mountain overlooking Hebron." He carried a city's gate, doors, posts, and locking bar, on his shoulders, out of Gaza and up into Israel's hill country, and left it on a mountaintop like a signature. The ambush at dawn found an open hole where the gate had been. That is Samson at his ceiling: careless about why he was in Gaza, untouchable in what he could do there.

"Some time later, Samson fell in love with a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah." The text says he loved her. It is the only woman in Samson's life the book names, the wife at Timnah went unnamed and so did the woman at Gaza, and it is the only time the book says Samson loved anyone. The lords of the Philistines came to her with a contract priced like a king's ransom: "Entice him and find out the source of his great strength and how we can overpower him to tie him up and subdue him. Then each one of us will give you eleven hundred shekels of silver." Five lords, eleven hundred shekels each, fifty-five hundred shekels of silver for one secret, more than three times the weight of gold Gideon took for his ephod, offered to a woman in a valley on Israel's border. She took the contract, and she asked him the question straight out, in nearly the lords' own words: "Please tell me the source of your great strength and how you can be tied up and subdued."

Samson lied to her three times, and the lies are told here in their pattern, because the pattern is the diagnosis. First: "If they tie me up with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, I will become as weak as any other man." She tied him with seven fresh bowstrings while Philistines hid in her room, and called out the ambush phrase: "Samson, the Philistines are here!" He snapped the bowstrings "like a strand of yarn seared by a flame." Second, after her reproach, "You have mocked me and lied to me! Now please tell me how you can be tied up," he upgraded the lie slightly: "If they tie me up with new ropes that have never been used, I will become as weak as any other man." New ropes, hidden men, the same shout, and he snapped the ropes "like they were threads." Third time, the lie moved to his head: "If you weave the seven braids of my head into the web of a loom and tighten it with a pin, I will become as weak as any other man." She wove his hair into a loom while he slept, pin and web and all, and shouted again, and he woke and walked off with the loom. Each lie brought the secret closer to the surface. The third one was about his hair and his sleep, one step from the truth, told to the woman who had already betrayed the first two answers to men hiding in her room. Samson could count. He stayed anyway. That is the riddle of Samson that he never posed at a feast: not how he could be so strong, but how a man who tore a lion apart could not walk out of a room he knew was a trap.

Her fourth approach changed weapons, from curiosity to love itself. She threw his own claim back at him, how can you say you love me "when your heart is not with me? This is the third time you have mocked me and failed to reveal to me the source of your great strength!" And she kept at him: "Finally, after she had pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death, Samson told her all that was in his heart." Sick to death is the text's phrase for what seven days of tears had done at Timnah and daily pleading did at Sorek. His tongue was the weakest muscle he had.
