"My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man."

Delilah knew the sound of the truth when it finally came. When she realized he had revealed to her all that was in his heart, she sent this message to the lords of the Philistines: "Come up once more, for he has revealed to me all that is in his heart." The lords came up with the silver in their hands. And she lulled him to sleep on her lap, the safest place he knew, and called a man in to shave the seven braids off his sleeping head. "In this way she began to subdue him, and his strength left him." Then she called out the phrase for the fourth time, the phrase that had always been a false alarm: "Samson, the Philistines are here!" He woke and thought the thought that had always been true before: "I will escape as I did before and shake myself free." And the narrator sets the saddest line in the book beside it, level and quiet: "But he did not know that the LORD had departed from him." His strength had never been his hair, or his arms. It had been a presence, and the presence could leave a man while he slept, and he could wake reaching for it and find it gone.

The Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes, the eyes that had done all his choosing, by his own rule that a woman was pleasing to his eyes, now answered by darkness. They brought him down to Gaza, the city whose gates he had carried off, and bound him with bronze shackles, real metal for the man ropes could not hold, "and forced to grind grain in the prison." Grinding was the work of women and slaves, pushing a millstone in circles. The deliverer of Israel spent his days walking in a circle in the dark, doing the labor of the household he might have had, in the stronghold of the enemy he was born to break. And underneath the shackles, one quiet verse turns the whole story: "However, the hair of his head began to grow back after it had been shaved."

The lords of the Philistines read the capture as theology and threw a festival for it, a great sacrifice to Dagon their god, with the verdict sung out loud: "Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands." When the crowd saw the blind prisoner, they praised their god in a fuller chorus: "Our god has delivered into our hands our enemy who destroyed our land and multiplied our dead." And when the drinking had made their hearts merry, they had the idea that pride always eventually has: "Call for Samson to entertain us." Bring out the blind strongman and let him perform. They set him between the pillars of the temple to be laughed at, and the temple was full, every lord of the Philistines in attendance, and about three thousand men and women on the roof watching the show.

Samson asked the servant boy who led him by the hand for one small thing: "Lead me where I can feel the pillars supporting the temple, so I can lean against them." A blind man wanting to rest against a pillar. Nobody in the building understood what he was measuring. Then the prisoner prayed, the second prayer of his life in this book. His first, at Lehi, had asked God for water after a victory and complained while he asked. This one asks for his vengeance by name and calls it that: "O Lord GOD, please remember me. Strengthen me, O God, just once more, so that with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes." The text does not upgrade his motive. He does not pray for Israel, or for the forty years, or for the deliverance he was born only to begin. He prays for his eyes, once more, and God answers the prayer as prayed.

He braced himself against the two central pillars, "with his right hand on one pillar and his left hand on the other," and said his last words, which are a request to be included in the death he was about to deal: "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he pushed with all his might, and the temple came down on the lords of the Philistines and everyone in it, roof, gallery, and congregation together. The narrator weighs the life in one sentence and closes the account: "So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life."

His brothers and his father's whole family came down to Gaza to claim the body, the family that had traveled down to Timnah to arrange his marriage and watched his whole arc from a distance. They carried him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol, where the Spirit had first begun to stir him, in the tomb of his father Manoah. "And he had judged Israel twenty years." The deliverance he was commissioned to begin, he began: five lords of the Philistines died in one afternoon, more of the enemy's leadership than any judge before him had killed at one stroke, and he did it blind, shackled, and praying for his own revenge. The book refuses to tidy him. He is the strongest deliverer and the least disciplined man in its pages, chosen from the womb and careless with everything he was chosen for, and God used him anyway, beginning a deliverance he never finished and would not live to see finished.

Samson is the last judge the book will follow. What comes next is not a deliverer story at all. The final five chapters step back from the cycle and show Israel from the inside, in its houses and shrines and roads, and they are set early in the period, in the days when Moses' own grandson was still alive to be hired as a priest. The refrain that will sound over them is the bleakest diagnosis the narrator owns: there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

title: Micah's Gods, and Dan's Migration
subtitle: Judges 17 to 18
description: A stolen fortune becomes an idol, a Levite is hired at ten shekels a year, and a tribe steals a shrine on its way north.
paragraphs: The last five chapters of Judges contain no judge, no oppressor, and no cry. They are placed at the end of the book, and the first thing to know about them is that they did not happen at the end of the era. Their own markers put them early: the priest in this story will turn out to be a grandson of Moses, and in the next story Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, is still ministering before the ark. These are tales from the first generation or two after Joshua, kept for the end of the book the way you save the diagnosis for after the symptoms. The narrator hangs a refrain over them like a sign over a door: in those days there was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Samson's personal creed, now posted as the condition of the whole nation.

A man named Micah, from the hill country of Ephraim, stole eleven hundred shekels of silver from his own mother. The sum is the one the lords of the Philistines offered Delilah, each of them; in this story it is a widow's whole fortune. She uttered a curse on the thief, not knowing he was her son, and Micah, who heard the curse, came and confessed: "I have the silver here with me; I took it." His mother reversed the curse on the spot into a blessing, "Blessed be my son by the LORD!", and then she did the thing that defines the age. She dedicated the recovered silver to the LORD, in so many words, for the making of an idol: "I wholly dedicate the silver to the LORD for my son's benefit, to make a graven image and a molten idol. Therefore I will now return it to you." To the LORD, for an idol. The sentence does not notice its own contradiction, and neither does she. She took two hundred of the shekels to a silversmith, and the images were made and installed in Micah's house, where he already kept a private shrine complete with an ephod and household idols, and had ordained one of his own sons as his priest. A stolen fortune, a mother's blessing, a homemade god, a boy priest. The narrator posts the sign over the scene: "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."

Then a genuine Levite walked into the story, a young man from Bethlehem in Judah who had left home "to settle where he could find a place," a priest of the LORD's own tribe drifting for work. Micah hired him the day he arrived, offering him the title and the terms: the young man was to "be my father and priest," at a wage of "ten shekels of silver per year, a suit of clothes, and your provisions." Ten shekels a year, for a Levite, bought with the leftovers of stolen silver a silversmith had already skimmed. The Levite agreed and settled in and became like a son of the house, and Micah ordained him over the shrine, and Micah's conclusion from the whole arrangement is the theology of the era stated as a proverb: "Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest." A real Levite on the payroll made the idols official, in Micah's accounting. God could be hired, housed, and pointed at a shrine, and His goodness could be known in advance from the staffing.

The tribe of Dan enters the story still homeless. "In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of the Danites was looking for territory to occupy. For up to that time they had not come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel." Dan's coastal allotment had never been taken; the Amorites had penned the tribe into the hills back in chapter 1, and Samson's lifetime of skirmishing had not changed the map. So Dan sent five men of valor from Zorah and Eshtaol, Samson's own towns, to spy out a new country, and on their way north they lodged at Micah's house and recognized the young Levite's voice. They interrogated him: "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?" He told them plainly: "Micah has done this and that for me," he replied, "and he has hired me to be his priest." Then the spies asked the hired priest for the service he was hired for: "Please inquire of God to determine whether we will have a successful journey." And the priest told them: "Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey." Whether God had spoken any such thing, the text does not say. The oracle cost nothing and pleased the customer, which in Micah's shrine may have been the same thing.

The spies went on to Laish, at the far north, and found a city living the way Israel was supposed to make its neighbors afraid to live: secure, "quiet and unsuspecting," with nothing lacking, no oppressive ruler, far from Sidon and holding no alliance with anyone. They came home with the good spies' report, in the very cadences Caleb once used for the promised land: "Come on, let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and it is very good. Why would you fail to act? Do not hesitate to go there and take possession of the land! When you enter, you will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land, for God has delivered it into your hand. It is a place where nothing on earth is lacking." Every word of the conquest's faith, aimed at a peaceful city Israel had no quarrel with, no command against, and no claim on. The forms of devotion had survived intact. They were now available for hire, like the priest.

Six hundred Danites marched north with their families, armed for war, and camped at Kiriath-jearim, a place called Mahaneh-dan, the camp of Dan, to this day, the same camp name where the Spirit had stirred Samson. From there they came to Micah's house, and the five spies briefed their brothers with the inventory: "Did you know that one of these houses has an ephod, household gods, a graven image, and a molten idol? Now think about what you should do." What they did was efficient. While the six hundred armed men stood at the gate with the priest, the five went inside and took the graven image, the ephod, the household idols, and the molten idol. The Levite protested: "What are you doing?" The Danites made him a better offer than Micah's, and phrased it as wisdom: put your hand over your mouth, "and come with us and be a father and a priest to us. Is it better for you to be a priest for the house of one person or a priest for a tribe and family in Israel?" A promotion, from one man's shrine to a whole tribe's. "So the priest was glad and took the ephod, the household idols, and the graven image, and went with the people." Glad. He carried the gods out himself.

They set their children, livestock, and possessions in front of the column, expecting trouble behind them, and Micah came as expected, with the men of his neighborhood mobilized, shouting after his property. The Danites turned and played innocent with an army at their backs: "What is the matter with you that you have called out such a company?" Micah's answer is the most nakedly honest line in the appendix, a man telling the truth about what his religion was: "You took the gods I had made, and my priest, and went away. What else do I have?" The gods I had made. He knew where they came from; he had watched the silversmith pour them. They were his gods anyway, and with them gone he had nothing, which was exactly what he had had with them, minus the silver. The Danites dropped the innocence for a death threat: "Do not raise your voice against us, or angry men will attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives." Micah saw they were too strong for him, and turned and went home, and that is the last the book says of him: a man robbed of the gods he manufactured, by the tribe that would worship them for centuries.

The Danites came to Laish, "to a quiet and unsuspecting people, and they struck them with their swords and burned down the city." The narrator adds the sentence that measures it: "There was no one to deliver them, because the city was far from Sidon and had no alliance with anyone." Deliver is the book's word for what God did for Israel through judge after judge. Here it appears in the negative, for a city of strangers, because Israel had become the kind of danger Israel used to cry out against. They rebuilt the city and named it Dan, after their forefather, and set up Micah's idols as the tribal shrine. And then the narrator names the priest at last, and the name is the story's detonation, saved for its final verse: "The Danites set up idols for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, the son of Moses, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the day of the captivity of the land." Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses. The wandering Levite who sold his priesthood for ten shekels and a promotion was the grandson of the man who received the Law, and his sons inherited the idol's altar at Dan for generations, until the Assyrians emptied the land centuries later. And the closing note sets the two shrines side by side without comment: Micah's graven image stood at Dan "the whole time the house of God was in Shiloh." The true sanctuary and the stolen idol operated in parallel, in the same small country, for the entire age of the judges, and both were staffed by Levites, and Israel saw no crisis in it at all.

There is one story left in the book, and it makes this one look like a dispute over property. It also begins with a Levite far from home, in the same hill country of Ephraim, and a household, and a journey. It ends with a tribe of Israel nearly erased from the earth, by Israel.

title: Gibeah, and the War That Cost a Tribe
subtitle: Judges 19 to 21
description: A crime in Benjamin summons all Israel to Mizpah, and the oaths sworn there nearly erase a tribe from the nation.
paragraphs: The book's last story opens with the refrain, worn smooth by now: "Now in those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite who lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah." She was unfaithful to him and left him and went home to her father's house in Bethlehem, and after four months her husband went after her, the text says, "to speak kindly to her and bring her back," taking his servant and a pair of donkeys. Whatever passed between them, her father welcomed him gladly, and then the father began the friendliest delay in the book. Three days of eating and drinking became a fourth day, with bread to refresh his heart before the road. The fourth day became a fifth, "Please refresh your heart," until late afternoon. On the fifth day the father tried once more, the light already going: "Look, the day is drawing to a close. Please spend the night. See, the day is almost over. Spend the night here, that your heart may be merry. Then you can get up early tomorrow for your journey home." This time the Levite refused, and got up and left with the day nearly spent, a man, a servant, two donkeys, and a woman riding into the dusk because hospitality had eaten his margin of daylight.

Opposite Jebus, which is Jerusalem, the servant suggested stopping in the Jebusite city for the night. The Levite's answer is the sentence the whole story turns on, because every assumption inside it is about to be destroyed: "We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah." Foreigners were the danger; Israelites were the safety. They pushed on in the dark and came to Gibeah in Benjamin, and sat down in the city square, and discovered the first fact about Gibeah: "no one would take them into his home for the night." A traveler could sit in an Israelite town square at nightfall, with donkeys and luggage announcing him, and be left there. Only an old man, himself a sojourner from the hill country of Ephraim who worked fields outside the Benjamite town, came in at evening and took them in, with the one condition that names how dangerous the square itself was: "Peace to you," said the old man. "Let me supply everything you need. Only do not spend the night in the square." He fed the donkeys, they washed their feet and ate and drank, and the story slowed down for one paragraph of ordinary shelter, because what came next needed a house with a door.

While they were enjoying themselves, suddenly the wicked men of the city surrounded the house, pounding on the door, and demanded of the old man who owned the house: "Bring out the man who came to your house, so we can have relations with him!" The scene is Sodom, beat for beat, in a town of Benjamin: the traveler taken in, the mob at the door after dark, the demand for the guest. Only the address has changed, from the city God destroyed outside Israel to a city inside it. The old man went out and pleaded with his neighbors in the language of the guest-code: "No, my brothers, do not do this wicked thing! After all, this man is a guest in my house. Do not commit this outrage." And then, exactly as Lot had, he made the offer that exposes what the age had done to the men as well as the mob: "Look, let me bring out my virgin daughter and the man's concubine, and you can use them and do with them as you wish. But do not do such a vile thing to this man." The guest, a man, was to be protected at the price of the women. The mob would not listen. "But the men would not listen to him. So the Levite took his concubine and sent her outside to them, and they raped her and abused her throughout the night, and at dawn they let her go." The text does not decorate it. Her husband, the man who had gone to Bethlehem to speak kindly to her, put her out the door himself, and the narration gives the crime one sentence and gives her the last movement of the chapter: she crawled back to the house where her master was staying and collapsed at the doorway, and lay there until it was light, and when he opened the door in the morning to go out on his journey, "there was his concubine, collapsed in the doorway of the house, with her hands on the threshold." He told her to get up, that it was time to go. "But there was no response." He put her on his donkey and set out for home.

What he did at home is the act that summoned a nation. He took a knife and cut her body into twelve pieces, limb by limb, and sent the pieces throughout the territory of Israel, one for every tribe, a summons no herald could have matched. And the response the text records from everyone who saw it sets the scale: "Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!"

Israel spoke up in one body. All the Israelites "from Dan to Beersheba" and from Gilead assembled "as one man before the LORD at Mizpah," four hundred thousand swordsmen, the largest gathering of the era, and there was no judge over them and no king; there was a congregation doing what the cycle had never yet produced, unified national outrage. They asked how the wicked thing had happened, and the Levite testified. His account stands in the text beside chapter 19's own narration, and the two do not cover the same ground. He told the assembly: "I and my concubine came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night. And during the night, the men of Gibeah rose up against me and surrounded the house. They intended to kill me, but they abused my concubine, and she died." Then: "Then I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent her throughout the land of Israel's inheritance, because they had committed a lewd and disgraceful act in Israel. Behold, all you Israelites, give your advice and verdict here and now." What his testimony does not contain is the doorway, his own hands sending her out to the mob to save himself. The assembly heard the edited version, and the reader of the book has both. The verdict was immediate and unanimous: "Not one of us will return to his tent or to his house." They would go against Gibeah, and first they sent messengers through Benjamin with the demand any court would recognize: "Hand over the wicked men of Gibeah so we can put them to death and purge Israel of this evil." Justice, targeted at the criminals, with the rest of the tribe untouched. "But the Benjamites refused to heed the voice of their fellow Israelites." Benjamin chose its worst men over its brothers, mustered twenty-six thousand swordsmen from its cities plus seven hundred select men of Gibeah itself, and among them the seven hundred left-handers the book had promised, "each of whom could sling a stone at a hair without missing."

The war that followed did not go the way numbers or righteousness suggested it should. Israel went up to Bethel and inquired of God, and heard the oldest answer in the book: "Who of us shall go up first to fight against the Benjamites?" "Judah will be first," the LORD replied, the same appointment Judah received the day after Joshua died. Day one: Benjamin came out of Gibeah "and cut down 22,000 Israelites on the battlefield that day." Israel took courage, formed up in the same place, went up and wept before the LORD until evening, and asked whether to go again against their brothers, and the answer was: "Go up against them." Day two: Benjamin cut down eighteen thousand more. Forty thousand Israelites were dead in two days for demanding justice against rapists and murderers, at God's own direction to keep going, and the text offers no explanation on the spot. It shows Israel doing the only thing left: "Then the Israelites, all the people, went up to Bethel, where they sat weeping before the LORD. That day they fasted until evening and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD." Then they inquired a third time, and the narrator supplies the credentials of the moment, which are also this story's birth certificate: in those days the ark of the covenant was at Bethel, "and Phinehas son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, served before it." Phinehas, who had speared an Israelite man and a Midianite woman at Peor in the wilderness and turned away a plague, Aaron's grandson, still ministering. This war is an old man's war, a first-generation war; the whole appendix is. The question was whether to go out again "against our brothers the Benjamites, or should we stop," and this time the answer carried the promise the first two had withheld: "Fight, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand."

On the third day Israel fought Benjamin the way God had taught it to fight Ai, with an ambush, the only stratagem that had ever taken a walled Israelite-era city in the conquest. They arrayed against Gibeah as before, let Benjamin come out and draw them into a feigned retreat along the roads, killing about thirty as the trap was set, and Benjamin read the battle wrong out loud: "We are defeating them as before," said the Benjamites. The ambushers rushed Gibeah and put the whole city to the sword, and sent up the arranged signal, a great column of smoke, and the main body turned, "and the men of Benjamin were terrified when they realized that disaster had come upon them." They fled toward the wilderness and the battle overtook them on the roads and in the fields east of their own city: eighteen thousand fell that day in the pursuit, five thousand more cut down on the roads, two thousand at Gidom, twenty-five thousand and one hundred by the day's own count, "all men of valor." Six hundred Benjamites reached the rock of Rimmon and held out there in the wilderness for four months. And Israel completed the work past the battlefield, turning back through Benjamin's territory and putting to the sword every city, the people, the animals, everything, and burning the cities in its path. It had demanded Benjamin hand over a city's criminals, and Benjamin's refusal had widened the sentence to a tribe: twenty-five thousand dead, every town ash, six hundred men alive on a rock.

Then the victors sat down at Bethel and wept over what they had won, and discovered the trap their own oaths had built. At Mizpah, in the heat of the summons, Israel had sworn that none of them would give a daughter in marriage to a Benjamite. Now: "Why, O LORD God of Israel," they cried out, "has this happened in Israel? Today in Israel one tribe is missing!" The six hundred at Rimmon would die unmarried, and Benjamin, Jacob's youngest, Rachel's son, would end in a generation, erased not by any enemy but by the arithmetic of Israelite oaths. Grief produced a search for loopholes, and the first loophole was a second oath: anyone who had not come up to the Mizpah assembly was under sentence of death. The count was taken, and one town had never come: "no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp for the assembly." So the congregation sent twelve thousand of its most valiant men against an Israelite town that had committed no crime except absence, with orders in the language of the old conquest: "Go and put to the sword those living in Jabesh-gilead, including women and children. This is what you are to do: Devote to destruction every male, as well as every female who has had relations with a man." They found four hundred young women who had never known a man, and spared them, and carried them to Shiloh as wives for Benjamin. Four hundred women purchased with their whole town. The congregation sent a message of peace to Rimmon, and the six hundred came down and received the women of Jabesh-gilead, "but there were not enough women for all of them."

The second loophole was worse, and the elders designed it themselves. There was a yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, with the daughters of Shiloh dancing in the vineyards. The elders commanded the remaining Benjamites: "Go, hide in the vineyards and watch. When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out to perform their dances, each of you is to come out of the vineyards, catch for himself a wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin." And for the fathers and brothers who would come to complain, the elders had the legal theory ready: "Do us a favor by helping them, since we did not get wives for each of them in the war. Since you did not actually give them your daughters, you have no guilt." You did not give them; they were taken; the oath is intact. Everyone could recite why it was permitted, and no one in the text calls it anything but what it is, an arranged abduction at a feast of the LORD, engineered by the elders of Israel to outwit an oath they regretted. The Benjamites did it, carried away the number of women they needed, went home, rebuilt their burned cities, and settled in them.

"And at that time, each of the Israelites returned from there to his own tribe and clan, each to his own inheritance." The assembly that had gathered as one man dissolved into its inheritances, and the book of Judges closes with the line it has been building since the angel wept at Bochim, the refrain in full, as the final word on the era: "In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes."

That is where the book leaves Israel: not under a foreign oppressor, not crying out, not waiting for a deliverer, but quiet, and maimed by its own hands, having started the era unable to drive out the nations and ended it unable to stop destroying itself. And yet the series does not leave the era on this page. The next story in the order Joe set for this telling is a small one that happened somewhere inside these same years, in Bethlehem and Moab and back again, about a widow and her daughter-in-law and a man named Boaz, and it opens with the era's own timestamp: in the days when the judges ruled. After Gibeah, it reads like a light left on in the same dark country, and it begins with a famine and a family leaving Bethlehem, the house of bread, to go and live in Moab.
